title: The Fed waits for a recovery that can withstand higher mortgage rates
summary: On 18 September the Federal Open Market Committee kept monthly purchases of agency mortgage-backed securities at $40 billion and longer-term Treasuries at $45 billion. A year into the purchase programme, policymakers judged that the private economy had strengthened despite federal fiscal restraint. They still wanted more evidence that employment gains could persist as financial conditions tightened. Holding the purchase rate steady thus conveyed information about the Committee’s tolerance for a rise in borrowing costs. A steady instrument setting can contain substantial news when the market has placed some weight on a change. The decision itself records the setting; its size as a surprise depends on expectations immediately beforehand. (Statement, assessment and decision paragraphs.)

Mortgage rates help explain the apparent tension in the decision. Activity and fixed investment had advanced and housing had been strengthening. Yet a higher mortgage rate changes the payment on a loan available today, while past construction and spending reflect financing arranged earlier. A strong backward-looking housing indicator can coexist with weaker demand ahead. A sustained tightening of financial conditions could reduce hiring and slow further improvement even if the first data releases remained healthy. Fiscal restraint raised the price of a wrong call because it was already absorbing some of the momentum in private demand. The Committee acknowledged that downside risks had eased over the preceding year while giving weight to the new financing risk. Both judgements can hold at once. (Statement, first four policy paragraphs.)

The decision concerned three separate balance-sheet operations. The monthly figures governed additional purchases. Principal payments on the existing portfolio of agency debt and mortgage securities would continue to be reinvested in agency mortgage-backed securities. Maturing Treasuries would continue to be rolled over at auction. Treating the $85 billion purchase pace as the gross value of all the Desk’s transactions would conflate these flows. For mortgage investors the distinction matters because prepayments affect how much principal returns for reinvestment. For Treasury investors, a slower future pace would still leave an existing portfolio outstanding and a continuing reinvestment policy. An announcement can therefore change expected future duration supply even when current holdings do not fall. (Statement, purchase and reinvestment paragraph.)

The short-rate decision had its own conditions. The target range stayed at 0–0.25%. The unemployment threshold and the tests for projected inflation and longer-term expectations informed an expectation about the minimum duration of very low rates. The Committee also said it would consider other employment and financial indicators. Nothing in those conditions fixed a particular date for the first increase. Inflation was running below the longer-run goal while longer-term expectations had held steady. For a rates researcher, a decline in a ten-year yield on this announcement would leave several possibilities open: fewer expected short-rate increases in later years, less compensation for holding duration, or a change in the perceived downside risk to growth. A single yield cannot identify their contributions. (Statement, inflation assessment and federal funds guidance.)

The vote shows where the disagreement lay. Nine members supported the decision. Esther George was concerned about the risk that prolonged accommodation could encourage imbalances and eventually lift longer-run inflation expectations. That was a judgement about the cost of extending the policy, rather than a claim that observed expectations had already risen. It matters for interpreting the next release. Stronger hiring would bear on the majority’s evidentiary threshold; a change in longer-run inflation expectations or clearer evidence of risk-taking would also bear on the dissent. Changes in yields around the release can reveal repricing, but a trading-window observation alone cannot tell which argument market participants adopted. (Statement, final voting paragraph.)

questions.question: How much of the decision was already in the expected purchase path?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the last pre-meeting distribution of expected Treasury and agency purchases and compare it with the announced flows. Preserve both the expected timing of the first reduction and the subsequent pace. Two investors could expect the same initial reduction but very different cumulative holdings over the coming year, with different implications for duration supply.

questions.question: Was the strongest repricing at short or long maturities, and when?
questions.detail: Compare the two- and ten-year Treasury changes with short-dated policy instruments in the statement and press-conference windows separately. A change concentrated at long maturities would be consistent with a duration or medium-term policy channel. Inflation compensation, surveys or estimated term premia would be needed to distinguish that interpretation from changing expectations of growth and future short rates.

questions.question: Was the mortgage-rate increase large enough to interrupt an otherwise improving housing market?
questions.detail: Track purchase applications, refinance applications and subsequent permits separately. Compare regions or borrower cohorts facing different changes in financing costs, allowing for local employment and different starting house prices. The Committee was concerned with the persistence of the tightening. A short-lived dip in refinance activity and a broad decline in new home purchases have quite different implications for the employment outlook.
